p: On Ana's whiteboard they wrote what the State had to believe: that red wasn't common that night, and that some of the blood on his cuff came from the attack, not the bar.
That the guy from the bar, in Travis's last phone call to his sister, meant Luis. And that Luis was near the lot at a quarter past eleven.
At her kitchen table she wrote her own doubt across the top of an envelope, in capitals. Maybe he did it.

Phil Abrams, her father's trial lawyer, died in 2019, and his boxes came to Ana. In his 911 folder Dani read the rest of the neighbor's call: the man in red wore a ball cap. Her father never wore hats. When she read the cap, she didn't cross anything out.
Gene Vigil. The Commerce City detective who built the case in 2007. He's retired now, in Northglenn.
Ana Brennan. Everything she writes, she writes in pencil.
Joel Harlan. Dani's supervisor. He wants the case kept out of the building.
Luis Ruiz. On Wednesdays he and Dani play a chess game by phone, one move a call.
Teo Ruiz. Dani's brother. He keeps clear of anything to do with their father.
Lupe Ruiz. Six. She drew her grandfather on a purple horse and mailed it to Sterling.

Saturday, December 12. She was early, so she parked across the street from Gene Vigil's house in Northglenn and turned the engine off. Ranch house. Brick halfway up, siding the rest. A basketball hoop over the garage with no net on it. One string of Christmas lights ran along the gutter and quit halfway across, where a ladder still leaned against the house.
Ana had found him. Retired in 2016 and still in the phone book. She'd sent him a letter on her letterhead, and a week later he'd answered, though not really to Ana.
What Dani hadn't told Ana was that she knew him.

Sunday, October 28, 2007, a little after three in the afternoon. Two men at the front door. Her mother in her robe, up early from sleeping off a night shift. The younger detective sat in the living room with her father. The older one would talk to him after. The older one, the one with the mustache, asked Dani if she'd show him the basement. She offered him a glass of water first. She'd been raised to.

He'd stood in front of the washer with his hands in his coat pockets, like he didn't want to touch anything, and asked who did the laundry in this house. She told him. Her mom, Mondays. Then she'd asked him something, and she could still hear how high her voice was. Is my dad in trouble? I'm just trying to figure out a night, hon. He'd carried the jacket up the stairs in a brown paper bag.

Her prep book was on the passenger seat. Marking her page was the envelope from Thursday night, NEEDED and ENOUGH and the thing in capitals across the top. She didn't take it out. She looked at the half string of lights and at the clock, 9:48, and opened the note again.

Snow on Federal tonight, the wet kind that's gray before it lands. The laundromat has its door propped, so half the heat goes out onto the sidewalk, and somebody's kid is sitting in the doorway watching it go. Dicta took the radiator side of the rug. Pencil.

A flaw question hands you an argument that doesn't work and asks you to say why. Not whether the conclusion is true. Not whether you like the premises. The test lets you treat the premises as true. Your job is the step from them to the conclusion, and what's wrong with it.

So the order doesn't change. Find the conclusion. Find the reasons. Then look at the gap between them and ask what the author took for granted. Most flaws are an assumption with a bad reputation: the author needed something, never said it, and it isn't safe.

Wrong answers come in a few kinds. Some describe a mistake the argument never made. Some attack a premise, which is the one move the question already told you not to make. And some are true about the argument and still aren't the error. Those cost people the most. "It relies on a single witness" is true of plenty of good arguments. Is relying on one witness what goes wrong in this one? Ask that of every choice, out loud if you have to.

So say the flaw yourself before you look. One plain sentence: it assumes this, or it ignores that. Then go find the choice that says your sentence in the test's words. Look at the choices first and five well dressed descriptions will talk you out of what you saw.

How the exam asks it. Flaw stems say the reasoning is flawed because the argument does something, or that it's most vulnerable to criticism on certain grounds. Each choice describes a move. Check two things: did the argument make that move, and is that where it fails?

The same few shapes turn up so often that people name them. The names help you see faster. They won't win you a point alone, because the test describes the mistake in plain words, so learn what each one does.

The group and the member. What's true of a crew as a whole isn't automatically true of each man on it. A crew can win a safety award with one careless man on it. It runs the other way too. A team of strong players can still lose.

Fits isn't shows. Facts that fit one explanation usually fit others, and a description that fits a whole crew can't pick out one man on it. Ask what else would leave exactly these facts behind. If something would, the argument hasn't earned its conclusion.
One reason. Somebody did a thing, and the argument picks one reason for it and acts like there's no other. People wash jackets for more than one reason.
Nobody said otherwise. No evidence that something happened isn't evidence that it didn't, least of all when nobody looked. Before you lean on a silence, ask who was asked.
The source. The argument goes after the person who made a claim: their job, their temper, what they'd gain. Who said a thing can be a reason to check it. It can't make it false.
After, so because. One thing followed another, so the first caused the second. Maybe. Something else may have caused both, or it's chance. You'll meet this one again with numbers attached.
And last chapter's pair. A requirement treated as a guarantee, or a guarantee treated as a requirement. You know that one.

How the exam asks it. You'll rarely see a Latin name in a choice. You'll see the move described: "takes a lack of evidence for a claim as showing the claim is false," or "presumes that what is true of a group is true of each member." Match the description to the argument, not to a label you remember.
Two more shapes, and you've met one of them already. The coat on the bus.

A word changes jobs. The argument uses a word one way in a premise and another way in the conclusion, and the step only works if you don't notice the switch. The witness said light and meant pale. The argument heard light and meant thin. Nothing else in it was wrong, which is exactly why you sat on it for eleven minutes. When an argument feels airtight and still wrong, find the word that shows up twice and ask whether it means the same thing both times. Travis said the guy from the bar. In his mouth that could be any man who'd been inside. In the State's case it's the one man he fought. Same five words, two meanings.

The answer goes in first. The conclusion is hiding in one of the premises, so the argument proves what it started with. Run the State's case backward and you can hear it: the jacket in the lot was his because he was the man in the lot, and he was the man in the lot because of the jacket. Nobody ever said it that plainly. Nobody had to. Each half leaned on the other. Here's the test. Would anybody who doesn't already believe the conclusion believe the premise? If not, it's going in a circle.

How the exam asks it. A shifting word shows up in the choices as a key term used in two different senses. A circle shows up as an argument that takes for granted the very thing it sets out to show, or restates its conclusion as a reason.

A method question gives you an argument, which may be perfectly sound, and asks how it works. Describe the moves, not the topic. Pretend somebody took every noun out of the argument, and tell them what's left.

A few moves come up over and over. Analogy: this case is like that one, so treat it the same. Generalizing from experience: it happened in the cases I've seen, so it happened here. Counterexample: you said every, here's one that isn't. Ruling out alternatives until one is left. Showing that the other side's evidence doesn't support what they think it does.

Read method answers word by word. They're abstract, and each word has to match something the author did. If a choice says the author questions a source's reliability and nobody's reliability came up, it's out, however well it fits the mood.
Keep one thing from tonight. A single counterexample is enough to sink a claim about every case. It isn't enough to show the claim is usually wrong. Not always and usually not go in separate drawers.
Method and flaw are cousins. A flaw choice is a method choice with the mistake written into it. If you can say how an argument works, you're most of the way to saying where it breaks.

How the exam asks it. Method stems ask how the argument proceeds, or which one describes the technique the arguer uses. Say the moves to yourself before you look, then test each word of each choice against the stimulus.
Reading Comprehension asks the same kind of thing about whole passages. What's the author's attitude? How is the passage built? Why is this sentence here?

For attitude, hunt the words that aren't facts. Adjectives. Hedges. The "surely" and the "admittedly." Authors on this test rarely gush and rarely sneer, so the right answer is usually moderate and often two sided, like qualified approval or measured doubt. A writer can have an attitude by never hedging at all. A report that puts every inference in the same flat voice as every observation has a tone. It's certainty.

For organization, write a few words in the margin beside each paragraph saying what job it does, not what it's about. States the usual view. Shows its problem. Offers another. Then find the choice that lists those jobs in that order. Wrong answers get the order wrong, or give a paragraph a job it never does.
Function is the same question at the size of one sentence. Cover the sentence with your thumb and read around it. What stopped working? That's its job.

Purpose is the same question one size up: why did the author write the whole thing? The primary purpose answer starts with a verb, and the verb does most of the work. Describe, explain, argue, challenge, compare. Then it needs an object that covers the whole passage, not one paragraph. Say a passage spends a paragraph on why fewer children in a mountain valley grow up speaking its old dialect, the usual story being television, a paragraph on school records that track the decline more closely, and a last paragraph saying turning off the television alone won't bring the dialect back. The author's purpose is to challenge the usual explanation, offer a better one, and draw what follows from it. Two or three verbs, because the author did two or three things.

The usual traps are the wrong size or the wrong strength. To describe school records is one paragraph, not the passage. To prove television never mattered goes further than the author did. And hold the verb up against the tone. An author who lays out two views and picks neither wrote to describe, and a choice that says defend is gone on its first word. For a variation, take the same passage and cut the last paragraph. Now nobody draws a lesson. The purpose drops to explaining that a decline had a different cause than people thought, and a choice that says recommend a policy has added a paragraph that isn't there.

How the exam asks it. Attitude stems ask which choice best describes the author's attitude, or a named person's. Organization stems ask which choice most accurately describes the passage's structure. Extreme attitudes and choices that shuffle the paragraphs' order are the usual traps. Primary purpose stems want a verb that fits the whole passage at the author's strength.

Some flaws live in the big picture: a cause nobody checked, a sample that picked itself. Others live in one small word, and those are the ones people read straight past. Here are the small word flaws, then one argument broken four ways so you can hear the difference.

The backward arrow. A rule says if A, then B. The argument has B and concludes A. Every licensed electrician passed the state exam, and Rafi passed the state exam, so Rafi is licensed. Maybe he never applied. The test describes it as treating something required as if it were enough, or as mistaking a condition that's needed for one that guarantees.

The denied front. Same rule, and the argument has not A and concludes not B. Every licensed electrician passed the exam, and Rafi isn't licensed, so he didn't pass. He may have passed last week and be waiting on the paperwork. The test calls this inferring that the result won't happen because one way of getting it didn't. It's the same confusion as the backward arrow, wearing a coat.

The climbing counting word. Some of the residents oppose the plan, so most do. Most of the residents oppose it, so all of them do. Each one climbs a rung the evidence didn't. Its cousin slides the other way: some of the residents support the plan, so some don't. Some is at least one. It never says not all.

The climbing conclusion. The evidence makes something likely, and the conclusion calls it certain. Or the evidence shows something could happen, and the conclusion says it will. The test words this as treating a possibility as a certainty, or as drawing a stronger conclusion than the evidence allows. Hold the conclusion's verb up against the premises' verb. If the verb grew, that's the flaw.

The beaten argument. Somebody gave a bad reason for a claim, so the claim is false. The landlord says the furnace is fine because it's new, and new furnaces break all the time, so the furnace must be broken. Knocking out a reason doesn't knock out the claim. You've shown the landlord didn't prove it. The furnace could still be fine.

Now one argument broken four ways. Start with a good one. Every dryer serviced in May passed inspection, and dryer six was serviced in May, so dryer six passed. Fine. Version one: dryer six passed inspection, so it was serviced in May. Backward arrow. Version two: dryer six wasn't serviced in May, so it failed. Denied front. Version three: most dryers serviced in May passed, and dryer six was serviced in May, so dryer six certainly passed. Most can't carry certainly. Climbing conclusion. Version four: the owner said dryer six passed because the repairman is careful, and the repairman isn't careful, so dryer six failed. Beaten argument. Four flaws, one dryer, and each of them turns up on the test in plain clothes.

When you describe a flaw before you look at the choices, describe the small word too. Not just it assumes too much. It goes from most to all. It turns the arrow around. The choices are written at that level, and the wrong ones are usually one word off from the right one.

How the exam asks it. Flaw choices for these say the argument mistakes a condition required for something as enough to bring it about, infers that a claim is false because an argument for it is weak, or draws a conclusion stronger than the evidence supports. Check the small words in the argument before you trust a choice that sounds right.
A flaw, all the way through.

One whole flaw question, slowly. A bakery owner says this. Our new cardamom buns have been a success. We bake them only on Saturdays, and every Saturday since we started, all two hundred have sold by noon, and a card at the register found that nine in ten buyers loved them. So we should bake two hundred every day of the week.

Conclusion: bake two hundred every day. Premises: Saturdays sell two hundred, and the buyers liked them. Now say the gap before you look. Saturday might be special. Maybe two hundred sell because it's the only day you can get them, and seven days of buns would spread the same two hundred buyers across the week. One sentence: it assumes what sells on one day a week will sell on every day.

Now the choices, the way they'd come. It relies on a card that never asked buyers how old they were. True, and beside the point, since age has nothing to do with the jump to every day. It fails to say how much the buns cost to make. Maybe a problem for the bakery, and not a flaw in the reasoning, since the conclusion is about how many will sell, and cost isn't in it. It assumes that the buyers who loved the buns will come back. The argument doesn't need that. It takes for granted that sales on other days would match sales on the one day the buns are offered. That's your sentence in the test's words. And it confuses a cause with an effect. Nothing here is a cause.

Notice where the time went. Saying the gap took ten seconds, and after that the choices sorted themselves. The two that cost people points are the true one about the card and the business one about cost. The first is about the argument and not about where it breaks. The second is about the bakery and not about the argument at all.
How the exam asks it. On a flaw question, write the gap in a few words in the margin before you read the choices. Then check each choice twice: did the argument do this, and is this where it breaks?
Ana had passed it across the desk Thursday with two fingers, like it might be wet. A sheet off a hardware store notepad, folded in thirds.

Note from Gene Vigil to Ana Brennan, received Tuesday, December 8. Ms. Brennan. Got your letter. I'll talk to Luis Ruiz's daughter. I won't talk to a lawyer, no offense to you, I've sat across from enough of them. I worked that case right, and I don't mind showing anybody how. She can come Saturday the 12th at ten. I'll have coffee on. Tell her I remember her. G. Vigil
She'd read it maybe thirty times. The last line, mostly. Ana had read it once, said Huh, and gone back to sharpening.
Ten minutes left in the car. Long enough to work out who was waiting at the top of that driveway.
What attitude does Gene's note show?
A. Confident he worked it right. Polite to her, but wary of any lawyer at all.
B. Friendly and open. He sounds glad to help the family find out what really happened.
C. Nervous. He sounds worried about what she might turn up in his old file.
D. Annoyed. He thinks the family is wasting his time with a closed case.
I worked that case right. I'll have coffee on. Both, in the same breath. He isn't expecting to lose anything this morning, and he's going to be nice to her while he doesn't. She gets out of the car.

That's the one. Pencil down. Author's attitude. Every part of it is on the page: "I worked that case right" is confidence, "I won't talk to a lawyer" is the wariness, and the coffee and "tell her I remember her" are the courtesy. An attitude can be two sided when the text is.
Decision two. Every one of them.

He opened the side door of the garage before she could knock. Seventy two, heavy through the shoulders still, a cardigan buttoned wrong by one. No mustache. He looked at her a second longer than people usually do.
You grew up, he said. Come in. It's warmer than it looks.

It wasn't. A space heater ticked by a workbench. One bay held a long car under a fitted cover, a Buick, she guessed from the shape. His wife's, she'd find out. Against the back wall stood a gun safe as big as a refrigerator. Two mugs and a thermos waited on the bench. He poured without asking how she took it.

Your lawyer thinks the jacket's no good, he said. I'll tell you what I told the DA in '07. I worked bar fights my whole career. More than I can count. The two who go at it inside are the two you find in the lot. Every one of them. Your dad went at it with Hensley inside. So I knew where to look.
She held the mug with both hands. Before she argued with him she wanted to say back what he'd done. Not whether it was right. How he'd gotten there.
A. "So you're saying my father was a violent man out looking for a fight that night."
B. "So you're saying I should just take your word. You've done this longer than me."
C. "So you're saying nobody else in that bar had any reason to hurt Travis Hensley."
D. "So you're saying this one went the way all the other bar fights you worked went."
That's what I'm saying. He looks almost pleased that she got it in one. She writes nothing down, but she keeps two words of it. Every one.

Right. Now say why. Method of reasoning. He generalizes from the bar fights he's worked to this one: it always went this way, so it went this way here. Naming the move is the whole question. Whether the move holds up is a different question, and you'll get to it.
Decision three. What happened, then what it means.
The safe took him two tries. Binders inside. Up top, skinny spiral notebooks, a rubber band on each bunch. He pulled a binder.
I kept a copy of everything I ever signed, he said. My wife called it a sickness. Found the page. Turned it around for her.

Commerce City Police Department, Investigations. Case summary, Detective G. Vigil, Monday, October 29, 2007. One. On Saturday, October 27, 2007, at about a quarter past eleven at night, Travis Hensley, 31, was struck in the head in the rear lot of the Night Owl Tap. He died at one forty in the morning. Witness C. Baca observed a male in a red jacket strike the victim and flee on foot. She did not see a face. Two. Bartender R. Galvan identified Luis Ruiz, 42, a regular customer, as the man who fought with the victim inside the bar at about ten twenty five. Galvan states Ruiz wore a red Platte Valley Refining jacket. Three. On Sunday, October 28, 2007, I interviewed Ruiz at his residence. Ruiz denied any altercation and stated he drove home alone at a quarter to eleven. Four. Ruiz's daughter, age 15, stated Ruiz wore the red jacket on Saturday and that she found it wet in the washer on Sunday morning. The jacket was collected and submitted to the laboratory. Summary: Ruiz fought the victim less than one hour before the assault. The red jacket worn by Ruiz matches the witness's description of the assailant. Ruiz denied the altercation, which the bartender contradicts. Ruiz washed the jacket before police contact. Probable cause exists to arrest Luis Ruiz for the assault and death of Travis Hensley.
Ruiz's daughter, age 15. Her own paragraph first, she couldn't help it. Then top to bottom again. This time she read for the shape of it.
A. It states its conclusion up top, then gives the evidence one point at a time.
B. It weighs two possible suspects against each other, then explains why it chose one.
C. It reports the investigation's findings one by one, then sums them up into one conclusion.
D. It lists four statements people gave police, then rates how reliable each one is.

That's how they taught us, Gene says. What happened. Then what it means. She looks at the white space between paragraph four and the summary. Everything above it is what people told him. Everything under it is his.

Good. That's how you read it. Organization. Four numbered paragraphs of findings, the assault, the bar, the interview, the daughter, then a summary that pulls them into one claim, probable cause. That's the structure, named by job and in order.
Gene topped off her coffee and didn't say anything. He let her read. She'd give him that.

Five sentences in the summary. She went through them the way Ana had taught her to go through anything, asking what each one was for. She stopped on the second. The red jacket worn by Ruiz matches the witness's description of the assailant.
A. It repeats what the witness said about the jacket and keeps it in the reader's mind.
B. It's the one line that puts Luis in the lot. The rest is about him and needs it.
C. It gives the reason Luis would have gone after Travis Hensley again outside.
D. It shows Luis lied to the police about what he was wearing that night.
She puts her thumb over that one sentence and reads the summary again without it. A fight. A denial. A washing. All about her father, and none of it in the lot. She lifts her thumb, and there he is.

That's the one. Pencil down. Function of a detail. The witness never names anyone, and the other summary lines are about Ruiz. This sentence is the only bridge between the man in the lot and the man in the report. Take it out and the rest has nobody to point at.
She looked up. He'd been watching her read. Not unkindly. Carefully, like a man watching a step he knows is icy.
Matches, he said. I wrote it because it was true. Your dad wore red. She saw red. You're going to tell me something's wrong with that.
A. "It was true. It matched every man on his crew too. A match like that can't pick one."
B. "Matching doesn't mean much when she saw it from across a dark street at night."
C. "So you're admitting the jacket was the only thing you ever really had on him."
D. "So it wasn't him. If it matched all those men, it can't have been him."

I knew about the crew, he says. It's in the first report anybody wrote. Several. He drinks his coffee. The crew didn't fight him. Your dad did. Then the fight's doing the work, she says. Not the jacket. He doesn't answer that.

Right. Now say why. Flaw. The summary treats a match as if it picked out one man. Red matched Luis, and it matched every man on his crew in that jacket. A description that fits many people can't single out one of them, so the match alone can't put Luis in the lot.
You remember me, he said. Not a question.

Had a mustache, had hair. Not quite a smile. You offered me a glass of water. You asked was your dad in trouble. I've thought about that more than you'd guess. He set the mug down. You walked me down to that basement and told me your mom did the wash on Mondays. You'd never once seen him do it. Man never washed a sock in his life, and he runs a load at midnight. Same night somebody dies in that lot. He's washing off what he did. Didn't need a lab for that.
Space heater, ticking. She'd been fifteen and polite, and it had been the most useful thing anybody said to him all week.
What's the flaw in how Gene reads the washer?
A. "I was fifteen years old. You shouldn't have had a kid walk you down to her own basement."
B. "He says he spilled beer on it, and my mother was at work that night. That's a reason too."
C. "Your own report has him lying about a fight. That's a reason to wash it, too."
D. "If he'd been hiding a killing, he'd have burned that jacket. He wouldn't have washed it."

He said he never touched anybody. So if he was lying about the fight, the fight's a reason to wash it. You had two reasons and you picked one. Gene looks at the covered Buick a while. Nobody picks the boring reason in a homicide, he says.

Good. That's how you read it. Flaw. He gave the washing one explanation and treated it as the only one. His own report supplies another: Luis had a fight to hide, the one he denied. Washing fits that just as well, so it can't show what happened in the lot.
He stood up. Not fast. Standing took a hand on the bench.

I didn't make anything up, he said. Every word in that report, somebody told me or I saw. I've had people stand in this garage and tell me I framed a man. I never once wrote down a thing that wasn't so. His neck had gone red above the cardigan.
And there it was in her own head, already built. He's this angry, so he's hiding something. So it's a lie. She could feel how good it would be to say.
A. "You worked for the people who needed him convicted, so of course you'd say that."
B. "I don't think you lied. I think you stopped. Show me what you wrote that week."
C. "I'm sorry. I didn't come here to fight. I'll take your word for how you ran it."
D. "You're this angry because you know you got the wrong man. You're lying to me."
Gene looks at her a long time. Stopped. He says it again under his breath. Doesn't sit back down. Turns to the safe.

That's the one. Pencil down. Flaw. A man can be angry and right. Going after him leaves his report standing. Grant that he wrote down only what was so, and ask what he didn't write down. That's the question his argument can't answer.

He'd shut the safe out of habit. He worked the dial again. The notebooks on the top shelf went back to 1981, one rubber band per year. He took down 2007 and opened it to a page he didn't have to hunt for, and that told her something too.

Gene Vigil's notebook, Sunday, October 28, 2007. Five past nine. C. Baca, 64. House across from the rear lot. Up with granddaughter, earache. Kitchen window. About a quarter past eleven. Male, red jacket, cap, and the word cap is struck through. Hit the victim with something. The victim went down. The subject ran north on foot. No face. Height? Couldn't say. Called 911 right away. In the margin: boy, with a question mark.
Cap. She said cap. I wrote it down. Then I crossed it out. Why? Everybody who knew your dad said he never wore a hat. Jacket fit. Cap didn't. I figured she got one thing wrong.
And boy? He looked at it a long time. I don't know. Something she said I meant to come back to. Did you? No.
He closed the notebook. Look. If there'd been some other man in red out there that night, somebody would've come forward. Nineteen years. Nobody ever called me. That tells you something.
Where does Gene's point about nobody coming forward go wrong?
A. "You're right. If nobody's come forward by now, there probably wasn't anybody."
B. "Nobody took their names. You can't count silence from people nobody ever asked."
C. "So you never looked for anybody else. Not one other man, the whole time."
D. "The man who did it was never going to call you. That part's no surprise."

Names not obtained, he says. He knows the line. His own name's on the one under it. Archuleta was a rookie. The bar emptied out before he got his car door open. He doesn't say anything else. He doesn't put the notebook away yet, either.

Right. Now say why. Flaw. No one coming forward is treated as evidence that there was no one. But the patrons were never identified or asked. Silence only counts against something when someone was in a position to speak up and was looked for.
He'd put the notebook back in the safe before she left. It stays here, he'd said, and spun the dial, and walked her to her car. The lights on the gutter still stopped halfway.
Monday, December 14, Joel stopped at her desk on his way to court. Still keeping it out of the building? Every page. Good. Two knocks on her desk, his verdict knock, and he was gone down the hall.

Tuesday, December 15, she ran her first timed section on the 5:40 bus home. Twenty five questions out of the back of the prep book, thirty five minutes on her phone's timer, no pausing it at red lights. She was on pace by Colfax. Question eighteen was about a coat. A witness said the thief had worn a light coat, and the argument went on from there to a man whose coat was thin, and something in it was wrong, and she couldn't find what. She read it four times. A coat in a question was never going to be just a coat for her again. The timer went off two stops from home with four questions she'd never even read.
Wednesday's call was twelve minutes of chess and the weather in Sterling. She didn't tell him about Vigil. She'd tell him when she knew what to say.

Thursday, December 17, Ana's whiteboard still had the four lines under the long one. Line two, SOME OF THE BLOOD CAME FROM THE ATTACK, NOT THE BAR. Line four, NEAR THE LOT AT 11:15. Dani had written what she could remember of the notebook page on the bus, and Ana copied two words onto the board, off to the side, nowhere near the line. CAP. BOY?
Those aren't assumptions, she said. Those are things somebody didn't do.
Then, because she'd been carrying it since the ninth, Dani said, Pa says you wrote him. After 2010. Two pages.

The pocketknife stopped. Ana frowned at the pencil, like it had said it. He told you that. He said most of them don't write. Most of us don't. She finished the point and blew the shavings off. I wrote it three times. The first two were about the law. What the third was about, she kept. Gene's 2007 summary came out of Phil's box. She read it on her feet and handed it back in her regular voice.
Forget what he says. How does he write?
A. Neutral. A cop writing down what people told him, and nothing more.
B. Unsure. You can tell he knew underneath that his case was thin.
C. Certain. He writes what he concluded in the same flat voice as what he saw.
D. Angry at my father. He'd decided he hated him before he wrote a word of it.

Certain, Dani says. What he decided sounds just like what he saw. Not one may in it, Ana says. Cops are supposed to write like that. Juries aren't supposed to read like that. She taps the word matches. Twelve people heard that read out loud in his voice.

Good. That's how you read it. Author's attitude. The tone lives in what's missing. No hedges, no "appears," no "may." The inference that the jacket matches sits in the same plain register as the time of death. That's certainty.
She told Ana the other thing before she lost her nerve. Tuesday night she'd gone on the website and moved her test from January to June. Paid the fee. Clicked through it fast.

Ana put the pencil down. I told you I wouldn't be the reason. You're not. I ran a timed section on the bus and the clock beat me by four questions. I want to walk in there ready, not sorry. Ana didn't say anything at first. June, then. And you keep that one. I'll keep that one.

Ana held her hand out for the prep book and ran her pencil down the column Dani had marked on the bus. Seventeen right, four wrong, four blank at the bottom. You didn't miss these four, she said. You never got to them. Where'd the time go? Eighteen. A coat. Eleven minutes. Ana read it, and looked at her over it a second. Eleven minutes on one question. Flag it, move, come back. They all count the same. You'd have had four more swings and come back to this with time left. Staring at it never made one more right. She handed the book back. And light means two things in that one. That's your flaw. It's on tonight's list.
Then Dani told her about Gene's bar fights. Every one of them. The two who go at it inside are the two in the lot.

Ana leaned back. Nineteen ninety one. A bar on Colfax. A man said something about my sister, and I put my beer down his shirt, and he put me into the jukebox. You lost. Badly. I went out to my car and sat there and cried until I could drive. Twenty minutes later he came out, walked right past my car, didn't look. I didn't get out. She shrugged. Two people who went at it inside. Nobody waited for anybody. Nobody went at anybody in that lot.
Dicta lifted her head at the word jukebox and put it down again.
What did Ana's Colfax story do to Gene's argument?
A. "You showed he only believes it from spending his whole life on the job as a cop."
B. "You showed the pattern he's leaning on is usually wrong about bar fights."
C. "You showed my father went straight home after his fight, the same as you did."
D. "You gave him one case where it didn't happen. So it isn't every one of them."
One, Ana says. Against every, one's plenty. Pencil back in her hand. It doesn't tell you what your father did. It tells you Gene's rule can't tell you either.

That's the one. Pencil down. Method of reasoning. Counterexample. Gene claimed it happened every time. I gave him one case where it didn't, which is enough to defeat an every claim, and I claimed nothing more.
Monday, December 21, an envelope came from Sterling addressed to Dani, and inside it a second one, sealed, in her father's block printing. FOR LUPE.
Wednesday, December 23, seven, the basement stairs. Recording first. Then: Did it come? Monday. Don't let her think it's a dog.
She told him she'd gone to see Gene Vigil. The hiss went on long enough that she checked the screen. What'd he want? To show me how he did it. He said everything fit.
Another long one. Then maybe it did, mija, he said. Maybe that's the end of it. You've got your test.
Nobody's asking you to fix it. Nobody ever asked you.
She'd never heard him tell her to stop.
A. "Then maybe you're right, Pa. Maybe I should stop and just study for the test."
B. "The jury thought it all fit too, Pa. And juries get things wrong all the time."
C. "It didn't all fit. So it wasn't you. That's what I'm going to show them, Pa."
D. "Fitting isn't proving, Pa. All of it fits a dozen other men as well as you."
Quiet. A dozen, he says, like he's counting them. Then, so low she almost misses it: You sound sure. About the argument. He lets that sit. He doesn't ask what else.

Right. Now say why. Flaw. Gene's "everything fit" treats evidence consistent with a conclusion as proof of it. Each piece fits Luis, and each fits other explanations too. Until those are ruled out, fitting proves nothing.
Decision twelve. We had our guy.
Before she hung up he'd said, You going over to your brother's Friday? She said yes. Give her the horse. Tell him it's from me. A pause. Or don't. You know him.

Friday, December 25, Teo and Bianca's kitchen. Lupe opened the envelope at the table and pulled out a sheet of lined paper. A horse's head drawn in pencil on a little round base, carefully shaded. Underneath: This is a knight. It's the only one that can jump. Merry Christmas, Lupe. Grandpa.
It doesn't have any legs. It doesn't need legs. It jumps. Bianca put it on the fridge beside the one Lupe had drawn again for home, the purple horse, cap and all.

Teo had picked up the envelope. He turned it over once. The return address, the number. Dani waited for him to go out to the truck. He still crosses his sevens, he said. Then he put the envelope down on the counter, face up, and stayed at the table through dessert.
Monday, January 4, a note came through her mail slot. No stamp. Hardware store notepad, folded in thirds. I read it again. Saturday if you want. G.V. He'd known the house. Of course he had.
Saturday, January 9, Gene opened the side door before she knocked. Cold one, he said, and handed her the mug with the handle turned toward her.
I read the whole notebook, he said. Took me three nights.

Read your statement too. In with the rest. He turned the mug a quarter turn. I asked who did the laundry in that house. You told me. I wrote it down like you'd confessed to something. I was answering you. I know it. He didn't look up. I knew it then.
Whose car? My wife's. I start it Sundays. He looked at it. She'd have told me to give you the notebook the first time.
There's a few things in there I wrote down and never went back to. You want to know why? He didn't wait. We had our guy. You've got your guy, there's no reason to keep looking. That's how I thought.
She heard what it stood on, and said it back to him.
Which assumption does Gene's reason for stopping rely on?
A. "That what you set aside could never have shown you had the wrong man."
B. "That if you'd kept looking, you'd probably have found another man in red."
C. "That my father was guilty past any doubt anybody could ever raise about it."
D. "That the DA was pushing you to make an arrest before that weekend was out."
That's it, he says. He sits down heavily. And I didn't know what I'd set aside. That's the joke. You can't know a thing's no good if you never look at it.

Good. That's how you read it. Necessary assumption. Deny it: one of the dropped leads could have shown he had the wrong man. Then there was every reason to keep looking, and "no reason" collapses. It's modest. It doesn't claim Luis was guilty, only that nothing set aside could have changed the answer.

Nothing for a while. Heater ticking. Then he was up, the dial again, and down came 2007 from the top shelf, rubber band and all. Into a gallon freezer bag. He pressed the air out with the flat of his hand, like he was packing somebody's lunch.
He put it in her hands and kept his own on top of it a second longer than he had to. Give it to Brennan, he said. I'll say what's in it to anybody who asks me under oath.
You read my report closer than the jury did, he said. Closer than I did.

One more thing. It's not in there, because it wasn't evidence of anything. He sat back down on the stool. Monday night, after the arrest, I had him in the room six hours. He didn't ask for a lawyer. Didn't ask about your mother, or you. He asked me one thing the whole night.

'Was anybody else hurt?' Gene looked at the covered car. I said, what do you mean, anybody else? Not another word out of him till morning. Strange thing for a guilty man to ask. Strange for an innocent one too. So I quit thinking about it.
He walked her out. Halfway down the drive she looked back. Lights the whole length of the gutter now. He'd finished them sometime after Christmas, for nobody to see. No ladder.
Freezer bag on the passenger seat, on the prep book. Engine running, heater blowing on her hands, and she didn't put it in gear.
Her in Thornton. Mom at work. Teo at Abuela's. There wasn't anybody else.
